subject: Post-demo: integration notes — SDK/auth, routing, chat vs completions, streaming

Hi Karthik / Laura,

Thanks again for the demo this morning — the team found the latency numbers and routing flexibility compelling. A few follow-ups from the engineering side so we can scope next steps: 

- SDK setup: can you confirm recommended SDK (python + node) entry points for both hosted and private deployments? Any sample code for auth handshake?
- Auth: we have strict key rotation requirements and tenant-scoped tokens. Do you support short-lived bearer tokens + KMS-backed signing on the private deployment?
- Routing: want to route low-latency traffic to dedicated pools and fall back to hosted when capacity is low — any gotchas?
- Req/resp: our product team is debating chat vs completions for a mixed Q&A + tool-calling flow (structured JSON output + tool calls). Any guidance on max_tokens, stop behavior, and when to use streaming vs non-streaming?
- Embeddings/rerank: if we send 1k docs per query as candidates, what do you recommend for batching and model selection for embeddings + reranker?

I attached the call recording and a quick CSV of sample prompts for context. Would appreciate a short written recap with suggested SDK/auth snippets and a proposed schema for structured outputs.

Best,
Aisha

Subject: Re: Thanks — follow-ups from today's demo (SDK/auth/routing + req/resp Qs)

Hi Aisha — great questions. Below is a concise recap and actionable guidance; happy to hop on a quick tech call if you want code-walkthroughs.

1) SDK setup (recommended)
- Use the Redwood SDK (python/node). Entry points: RedwoodClient.generate() for completions-style single-turn, RedwoodClient.chat() for multi-turn conversational flows. Both support streaming via .stream() helpers.
- Example auth handshake (shortened):
  - Client fetches short-lived tenant token from your backend (signed by KMS).
  - Backend exchanges long-lived service credential for a Redwood scoped token via our token-exchange endpoint.
  - SDK uses the scoped token as Bearer on requests (rotate tokens every 15–60 min).
- We will share the integration-template.json with sample snippets (attached).

2) Auth + Private deployment
- Private supports KMS/HSM integration and tenant-scoped short-lived tokens. We recommend generating tokens in your control plane and using our token-exchange flow; Redwood verifies KMS signatures.
- For strict rotation, our recommended TTL is 15 minutes for high-security tenants; refresh via a silent refresh endpoint.

3) Routing and capacity fallbacks
- Policy model: route by policy keys (region, latency-tier, customer-tier). Define a primary routing target = Dedicated pool; fallback = Hosted catalog model.
- Gotchas: keep model variants matched (same tokenizer/model family) across fallback to avoid subtle tokenization differences; include version pin in routing policy to prevent regressions.
- We recommend a warm-cache grace period for stateful chat sessions — otherwise you may see initial longer latencies on fallback.

4) Request/response schema: chat vs completions, streaming semantics
- Chat (structured multi-turn): better when you need system/user/assistant roles, incremental tool-calling, and conversation state (KV cache benefits).
- Completions (single-shot): simpler for independent prompts or high-throughput scoring tasks.
- Structured output: use the tool-calling + JSON schema approach; include a top-level "output_type" and "tools" array. Example schema in attached integration-template.json.
- Tokenization / max_tokens: set max_tokens conservative to include expected JSON overhead + buffer. For 2k token contexts, limit completion to 512 tokens for cost-sensitive routes.
- Stop sequences: for JSON outputs use an explicit end delimiter (e.g., "
---END_JSON---
") as well as schema validation on the returned text. If you use streaming, flush tokens until you detect the delimiter, then stop the stream.
- Streaming semantics: stream is ideal for low-latency user-facing responses and tool-call partials (send partial JSON chunks). When using streaming with JSON, prefer line-delimited JSON chunks to make incremental parsing reliable. If strict atomic JSON is required, use non-streaming or stream only for human-visible portions and request the tool-call payload non-streaming.

5) Embeddings + rerank guidance
- Batch embeddings in groups of 256–512 depending on GPU memory and model (batch-size tuned). For 1k candidates: two-step approach = coarse embedding model (smaller, cheaper) for initial retrieval then a precision reranker (larger model) on top-k (e.g., top 50).
- Use dense embeddings + asymmetric rerankers (score only top candidates) to save cost. Redwood supports pinned model pools for rerankers in Dedicated to keep latency predictable.

Next steps:
- I attached integration-template.json and an architecture diagram (PDF) with recommended routing rules.
- Ben, can you confirm our recommended default max_tokens per model family for the reranker path?

If that looks good, we can spin up a sandbox tenant and share a short Getting Started snippet for your engs.

Thanks,
Karthik
Director, Solutions Engineering
Redwood Inference

Quick item — for the reranker path: recommend default max_tokens = 256 for score-only passes and 512 when you want explanation tokens included.

Also: example stop sequence for multi-turn JSON tool-calling: use ["\n---END_JSON---\n", "\n<END>\n"] — this lets you handle both explicit delimiters and short canonical markers.

-ben
